title: How to Build a Transformer
text:
In 2017, researchers from Google published a paper titled “Attention is All You Need”, which provided the backbone, called a transformer, for AI language models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and many others that we use so often in today’s world. The key mechanism that makes a transformer work is called the attention mechanism, and it can identify how things are related to each other. For a large language model like Claude, it can figure out how the words you type relate to each other. For example, if you asked Claude, “I heard about this machine learning model called a transformer, can you teach me about it?”, what would the word “it” refer to in the sentence? “It” refers to “transformer”, and the attention mechanism of the transformer is what figures that out. However, a transformer can learn patterns in anything we can quanitify, not just the words we send to our favorite chatbot. In fact, transformers are used all over in today’s world such as in video, audio and speech, robotics, science and medicine, search engines, and even self-driving cars. They are incredibly powerful, and with the help of AI, anyone can learn how to make and train one themselves. In this tutorial, we will learn how to identify when a transformer can be used, how to make certain design decisions that are needed for the transformer to work, and how to use AI to help us build it.

title: How to Build a Transformer
text:
Steps for Building a Transformer

Step 1:
First, we need to identify when a transformer is needed. A transformer is a mathematical process that works with numbers and then returns an output. The data that we use needs to be able to be divided into tokens. A token is a number or set of numbers that describes the thing we are trying to analyze. For ChatGPT, it is trying to analyze words, so each word or pieces of a word needs to be converted into a token, or set of numbers that describes that word. Once, we have all the tokens for a sentence, we can combine them all together and feed it into the transformer. Here are some ways that we can turn our data into tokens in different fields of study:



Field
Example
What counts as a “token”?




Language
Translation
Words or word pieces


Vision
Image classification
Image patches


Audio
Speech-to-text
Short slices of sound


Biology
AlphaFold
Amino acids


Weather
Forecasting models
Grid regions of the atmosphere



As an example, we are going to use pixels from images of hand-drawn numbers as our tokens.
On top of this, we use transformers when we are trying to classify something or output a number that can be checked with the correct answer. For example, in our hand drawn images, we want the transformer to be able to look at all the pixels and return the correct answer for what number has been drawn. To do this, we need to have the correct answer key available. This is called supervised learning.
{fig-alt=” ” width=80%}
Another criteria for using a transformer is when the data we are working with is very complex. More specifically, when the data is nonlinear, multicolinear (variables in the data are related to each other), and full of complicated interactions between variables. If you are unfamiliar with these concepts, ask an LLM to help you identify if these things may be a risk. We will not cover them in detail here, but they are very important statistical concepts to know.
Finally, we need to understand that transformers require a lot of data, or tokens, to train properly. The more complex the data is, the more of it we need. The hand drawn digit image data set has almost 1800 images to use, which is on the very low end of data sizes that we need for these types of problems. In many cases, we may need millions of tokens to train on. If you don’t have access to this much data, you may need to consider another way of analyzing it. As a simple rule of thumb, we need to take the number of parameters in the transformer, which we’ll discuss next, and multiply it by 10-20, and possibly more, to determine how many tokens you’ll need.


Step 2:
An important thing to consider is how we design the dimentions of the model. A transformer is really just a series of matrix multiplication. We get to decide how big these matrices are and how much information they can hold.
